title: On the Origin of Mass Ejection in Failed Supernovae
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Some high-mass stars likely end their lives in underluminous implosions that leave behind a black hole, known as failed supernovae (FSNe). However, neutrinos radiated during proto-neutron star formation generate a weak (Mach $\gtrsim 1$) shockwave in the outer layers of the star, which produces a unique transient as it breaks out of the dying star and signals its imminent disappearance. It was recently shown that there are two self-similar solutions that describe the propagation of this weak shockwave, and these solutions simultaneously contain outward-moving ejecta and fallback accretion onto the black hole. Here we show that the larger Mach number solutions are unstable, such that the Mach number of the shock grows with time $t$ and deviates from the self-similar prediction as $\propto t^α$, with $α\lesssim 0.1$, whereas the smaller Mach number solutions are stable. We also show that, above a critical mass loss that is readily achievable in core-collapse supernovae, the shock asymptotically strengthens and approaches the strong limit. Our results imply that it is the mass lost to neutrinos \textit{relative} to the mass enclosed by the shockwave, as well as the stellar density gradient where the shock forms, that primarily dictate its strength and the amount of material it ejects. These criteria explain why red supergiants, which have relative mass losses well in excess of the critical value at the time of shock formation, more readily eject material and create more luminous explosions compared to more compact progenitors.

AI.tldr: Neutrino-driven weak shocks in failed supernovae show stability dependence on their Mach number, with strong mass loss leading to stronger shocks and more ejecta, explaining why red supergiants produce brighter transients than compact stars.
AI.motivation: To understand the dynamics and stability of weak shockwaves generated by neutrinos in failed supernovae and how they affect the ejection of stellar material and observable transients.
AI.method: Analyzing the self-similar solutions describing the propagation of weak shockwaves during proto-neutron star formation and studying their stability and evolution over time under varying conditions of mass loss and stellar density gradients.
AI.result: The study finds that larger Mach number solutions are unstable and their shocks grow stronger over time, while smaller Mach number solutions remain stable. Above a critical mass loss, the weak shock strengthens asymptotically, approaching a strong shock limit. The mass loss relative to the enclosed mass and the stellar density gradient determine the shock’s strength and ejecta amount.
AI.conclusion: The shockwave behavior in failed supernovae, governed by neutrino-induced mass loss and stellar density gradients, explains the variability in ejecta production and luminosity of explosions, with red supergiants more likely to produce luminous transients due to their higher relative mass losses.

title: No model-independent evidence for a peak in binary black hole spin (mis)alignments
comment: 7 + 8 pages, 4 + 6 figures
summary: The degree of black-hole spin-orbit misalignment ("tilts") in the astrophysical population could be a powerful diagnostic to distinguish between binary formation in isolation, in dynamical environments, or in hierarchical triples. However, robust population-level spin tilt measurements are complicated by model misspecification as well as numerical and Poisson variance, ultimately owing to poor single-event constraints on tilts. Motivated by reports of a possible peak in the spin tilt distribution, we analyze the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA gravitational-wave transient catalog to test for preferred spin orientations at different black hole masses. We find that a peak in spin tilts is not statistically significant nor model independent. Since the data cannot be used to reliably identify subpopulations based on their spin tilt properties, we also consider a complementary approach: measuring the spin magnitude and tilt distributions at fixed mass scales. We find no confident correlation between mass and spin tilt, but we do confirm a confident correlation between spin magnitude and mass, corroborating recent analyses.

AI.tldr: Analysis of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data shows no strong evidence for preferred black hole spin tilt angles linked to mass, but confirms that spin magnitude increases with mass.
AI.motivation: To use black-hole spin-orbit misalignment angles ('tilts') as diagnostics for distinguishing binary formation channels.
AI.method: Analyzed the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA gravitational-wave transient catalog, testing for preferred spin orientations at different black hole masses and measuring spin magnitude and tilt distributions at fixed mass scales.
AI.result: No statistically significant or model-independent peak in spin tilt distribution was found; no confident correlation between black hole mass and spin tilt, but a confirmed correlation between spin magnitude and mass.
AI.conclusion: Spin tilt data from current gravitational-wave events do not reliably identify subpopulations or preferred orientations, but spin magnitude correlates with black hole mass, supporting recent findings.

title: An X-ray and optical spectral study of the changing-look narrow-line Seyfert 1 2MASX J0413-0050
comment: 16 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) showing dramatic spectral and flux variations, either due to changes in the accretion rate (changing-state, CS-AGN) of the supermassive black hole or in the line-of-sight column density (changing-obscuration, CO-AGN), have been classified as changing-look (CL) AGN. Here we present a peculiar source, 2MASX J0413-0050, first identified as a narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1s) galaxy in 2004. When re-observed twice in 2021, it showed a transition in the spectral type (towards a Seyfert 1.9) and the complete and mysterious disappearance of the Hbeta line while source was in a high accretion state. In the meantime, the X-ray flux decreased between observations taken in 2020 and 2022, and again in the most recent spectrum of 2023. Shortly after this, another optical spectrum revealed the re-emergence of both the narrow and broad Hbeta components (Seyfert 1.8). Despite the fact that it was not possible to retrieve the line-of-sight column density from the X-ray spectra, which would have helped in assessing whether this event could be attributed to a CO AGN scenario, the observational evidence does not necessarily support such an interpretation. J0413-0050 may have undergone several switch-on switch-off phases over the past 20 years, on an unknown timescale, which could have affected the accretion power and, consequently, the optical continuum and so the emission lines coming from the broad-line region (BLR). For these reasons, it is reasonable to classify this source as a CS-AGN. The case of J0413-0050 supports the hypothesis that NLS1s can indeed experience CL phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the AGN 2MASX J0413-0050, documenting its spectral transitions and variable fluxes that indicate multiple accretion-driven state changes, categorizing it as a changing-state AGN and demonstrating that narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies can exhibit changing-look behavior.
AI.motivation: To investigate the nature and classification of the peculiar active galactic nucleus 2MASX J0413-0050 showing dramatic spectral and flux variations.
AI.method: Multi-epoch observations in optical and X-ray bands were analyzed, including spectral line measurements and flux variations over nearly 20 years.
AI.result: The source exhibited spectral type transitions, disappearance and re-emergence of the Hbeta emission line, and variable X-ray flux without clear changes in line-of-sight column density, suggesting multiple cycles of activity related to accretion rate changes.
AI.conclusion: 2MASX J0413-0050 is best classified as a changing-state AGN driven primarily by accretion rate variations, supporting that narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies can undergo changing-look phenomena.

title: Multi-wavelength outburst activity from EP J174942.2-384834: a very faint X-ray transient discovered by Einstein Probe
comment: 31 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication on The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We report the discovery and multi-wavelength characterization of the Galactic transient EP J174942.2$-$384834, first detected by the Einstein Probe during a faint X-ray outburst in March 2025. Coordinated follow-up observations revealed two major outbursts and a rebrightening over a seven-month period. Broadband X-ray spectral modeling shows that the outburst emission was dominated by thermal Comptonization of very soft seed photons. The absence of a detected thermal disk component, together with the low inferred seed-photon temperature, is consistent with a cool and possibly truncated accretion disk. The X-ray spectrum remained consistently hard throughout the outburst activity, with a power-law photon index of $Γ\approx 1$-2, gradually softening as the flux declined. The optical/UV counterpart brightened in tandem with the X-ray emission and exhibited a blue continuum with broad Balmer absorption features. Together with the optical/UV - X-ray luminosity correlation, this supports a disk-dominated origin of the optical/UV outburst emission, with viscous heating likely playing a major role and irradiation possibly contributing, especially in the UV. No radio counterpart was detected, implying at most very faint jet activity. Taken together, the observed properties support the classification of EP J174942.2$-$384834 as a very faint X-ray transient black hole candidate. This study demonstrates the ability of Einstein Probe to uncover and characterize the faintest accreting compact objects in the Galaxy.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery and detailed multi-wavelength study of EP J174942.2$-$384834, a very faint Galactic X-ray transient likely hosting a black hole, characterized by thermal Comptonization from a cool accretion disk and disk-dominated optical/UV emission, with no strong jet activity, showcasing Einstein Probe's detection power.
AI.motivation: To discover and understand faint Galactic X-ray transients, particularly those that might be very faint X-ray transient black hole candidates, using multi-wavelength observations.
AI.method: Detection by the Einstein Probe of faint X-ray outbursts, followed by coordinated multi-wavelength (X-ray, optical/UV) observations and broadband X-ray spectral modeling to characterize the source properties and emission mechanisms.
AI.result: Identification of EP J174942.2$-$384834 as a very faint X-ray transient with two major outbursts and rebrightening over seven months, dominated by thermal Comptonization from a cool, possibly truncated accretion disk, correlated optical/UV brightening indicative of disk-dominated emission with viscous heating and possible irradiation, no radio jet detected, supporting its classification as a black hole candidate.
AI.conclusion: EP J174942.2$-$384834 is a Galactic very faint X-ray transient black hole candidate whose outbursts are caused by a cool, possibly truncated accretion disk with thermal Comptonization dominating X-ray emission; the optical/UV emission originates mainly from disk viscous heating and irradiation; the findings demonstrate Einstein Probe's capability to discover and study the faintest accreting compact objects.

title: Constraints on the inflationary vacuum and reheating era from NANOGrav
comment: 22 pages, 4 captioned figures. Comments are welcome
summary: NANOGrav and various pulsar timing array experiments recently reported evidence for a common red noise signal across millisecond pulsars. This signal exhibits Hellings-Downs inter-pulsar correlation patterns, providing compelling evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) signal. In general, such a background can come from several astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. Assuming such SGWB has an inflationary origin, we use latest NANOGrav 15-year dataset to constrain the inflationary parameters e.g., tensor spectral index ($n_t$), tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$), and explore the implications for the reheating phase through constraints on the reheating equation of state ($ω_{\text{re}}$) and reheating temperature ($T_{\text{re}})$. We find the preference for an extremely blue-tilted tensor spectrum $n_t=2.20^{+0.36}_{-1.2}$ and the radiation-like reheating scenario $ω_{\text{re}}=0.33^{+0.14}_{-0.36}$. Despite having no concrete evidence for the nature of the primordial vacua, the computation of gravitational wave (GW) sourced by tensor perturbations assumes the inflationary vacuum to be a Bunch-Davies vacuum. In this work, we examine modifications to the GW spectrum originating from the non-Bunch-Davies primordial vacuum. We find that NANOGrav observations favour a specific type of non-Bunch-Davies vacuum, known as the alpha-vacuum. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the observations strikingly narrow down the range of the parameter $α$ characterizing the vacua. On top of that, we find that a frequency-dependent parametrization of the vacuum parameter $α$ beyond a threshold frequency can yield a minimal solution to alleviate the blue-titled issue. Finally, we highlight the possibility of testing such frequency dependence of $α$ by probing the GW spectrum through future GW experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper uses NANOGrav data to constrain inflationary and reheating parameters of the stochastic gravitational wave background, showing preference for a blue-tilted tensor spectrum and an alpha-vacuum primordial state. Introducing frequency dependence in vacuum parameters may solve spectral issues and can be tested in future gravitational wave experiments.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the recent detection of a common red noise signal with Hellings-Downs correlations by NANOGrav and other pulsar timing arrays, interpreted as evidence of a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB), which could be of inflationary origin. The authors aim to use this data to constrain inflationary parameters and reheating scenarios and investigate the impact of non-standard primordial vacuum states on the GW spectrum.
AI.method: The authors analyze the latest NANOGrav 15-year dataset under the assumption of an inflationary SGWB. They constrain inflationary parameters (tensor spectral index, tensor-to-scalar ratio) and reheating parameters (equation of state, temperature). They also modify the GW spectrum by considering non-Bunch-Davies initial vacuum states, particularly focusing on the alpha-vacuum, and explore a frequency-dependent parametrization of the vacuum parameter alpha.
AI.result: The analysis prefers an extremely blue-tilted tensor spectrum (n_t ≈ 2.20), a radiation-like reheating equation of state (ω_re ≈ 0.33), and shows that the data strongly favor the alpha-vacuum as the primordial vacuum state. Constraints on the alpha parameter are tightened and a frequency-dependent alpha can alleviate the blue-tilted spectral issue. The model suggests future GW experiments could test this frequency dependence.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the recent NANOGrav signal supports an inflationary SGWB with a strongly blue-tilted tensor spectrum and radiation-like reheating, with the primordial vacuum better described by an alpha-vacuum state rather than the standard Bunch-Davies vacuum. Frequency-dependent vacuum parameters offer a promising avenue to resolve spectral tensions and can be probed by upcoming GW observations.

title: Moving-mesh simulations of spreading dynamics and local electron cooling in structured gamma-ray burst afterglow jets
comment: 21 pages (including Appendix), 22 figures, Accepted to be published in MNRAS main journal
summary: We present the results for the dynamics and emission profiles of axi-symmetric numerical simulations of structured gamma-ray burst afterglow jets, computed using the relativistic moving-mesh hydrodynamics code GAMMA. We find that the spreading of jets of average opening angle is moderately impacted by the initial steepness of the angular structure, although the effect disappears once the working surface of the jet substantially exceeds its initial width, and that the travel time of a sound wave across the front surface remains the best indicator of the onset of spreading also for structured jets. When computing the afterglow spectrum using a local cooling approach that traces the electron population following shock-acceleration, we observe a significant impact on the synchrotron cooling break. Similar to earlier results for top-hat jets, the cooling break is found to shift upward in frequency by well over a factor of ten relative to approaches that assume a global cooling timescale across the jet. The cooling break transition in the spectrum also becomes substantially smoother. For both local and global cooling, jet breaks become sharper with increasing frequency. Local cooling is found to initially lead to a steeper slope post jet-break. The local-cooling emission is shown to originate from a narrow frequency-dependent sized region behind the shock front, as expected, but in strong contrast to a global cooling approach.

AI.tldr: This study uses relativistic hydrodynamic simulations to explore the effects of jet structure and local synchrotron cooling on gamma-ray burst afterglow dynamics and emission, finding significant spectral and temporal differences compared to global cooling models.
AI.motivation: To better understand how the angular structure of GRB jets affects their dynamical evolution and afterglow emission properties, especially considering the impact of local versus global synchrotron cooling processes.
AI.method: Axi-symmetric numerical simulations of structured GRB afterglow jets were performed using the relativistic moving-mesh hydrodynamics code GAMMA. The afterglow spectrum was computed with a local cooling approach that tracks electron populations following shock acceleration.
AI.result: Jet spreading is initially influenced by angular structure steepness but becomes independent as the jet propagates. The synchrotron cooling break frequency is significantly higher under local cooling assumptions compared to global cooling. Jet breaks are frequency-dependent and sharper at higher frequencies. Local cooling results in emission from a narrow, frequency-dependent zone behind the shock front, unlike global cooling.
AI.conclusion: The dynamics of structured gamma-ray burst jets are moderately affected by the initial angular structure steepness, with jet spreading onset well indicated by sound wave travel time. Local cooling models significantly shift and smooth the synchrotron cooling break in the afterglow spectrum, differing notably from global cooling models. Jet breaks sharpen with frequency, and local cooling leads to a steeper post-break slope, with emission arising from a localized region behind the shock front.

title: Primordial Magnetic Fields at Cosmic Dawn: 21-cm Forecasts with HERA and SKA
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, submitted to PRD
summary: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) can enhance the abundance of low-mass halos during Cosmic Dawn by sourcing additional small-scale matter fluctuations. This enhanced small-scale power can accelerate early galaxy formation, shifting the timing of Lyman-$α$ coupling, X-ray heating, and reionization toward earlier times and imprinting correlated signatures on the global and fluctuating 21-cm signals. We extend the fast analytic framework {\tt\string zeus21} to include a physically motivated PMF contribution to the linear matter power spectrum, including radiative damping before recombination and magnetic-pressure suppression below the magnetic Jeans scale. The implementation preserves the speed and modularity of {\tt\string zeus21}, enabling efficient exploration of PMF parameter space. For $n_B=-2.9$, we quantify the impact of PMFs on early structure formation and 21-cm observables across a range of fiducial magnetic amplitudes, and forecast detectability with \textit{HERA} and \textit{SKA}. Combining 21-cm forecasts with external CMB priors, we find that upcoming experiments can probe PMFs through their impact on small-scale structure, providing constraints complementary to existing cosmological probes.

AI.tldr: This paper incorporates primordial magnetic fields into a fast analytic model to study their effect on early cosmic structure formation and 21-cm signals, forecasting that future 21-cm observations can detect and constrain PMFs alongside CMB data.
AI.motivation: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) can modify early structure formation by enhancing small-scale matter fluctuations, which affects key cosmic epochs observable in 21-cm signals, motivating the need to study their impact in detail.
AI.method: The study extends the zeus21 analytic framework to include PMF contributions to the linear matter power spectrum, accounting for radiative damping and magnetic pressure suppression effects, while maintaining computational efficiency for parameter space exploration.
AI.result: For a spectral index of n_B = -2.9, the paper quantifies how PMFs alter early structure formation and corresponding 21-cm observables, and forecasts detection capabilities with HERA and SKA, showing that 21-cm observations combined with CMB data can provide complementary constraints on PMFs.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming 21-cm experiments, combined with CMB priors, will enable probing of primordial magnetic fields via their influence on small-scale cosmic structures, offering new, complementary cosmological constraints.

title: Astrophysical X-Ray Polarization
comment: 21 pages, Invited chapter for the edited book "X-ray Polarimetry: Detection, Observations, Modeling and the Future" (Eds. Honghui Liu and Adam Ingram), Springer Singapore, expected in 2026
summary: X-ray polarimetry is now providing a new way to look at the high energy sky. The addition of two observables, polarization fraction and angle, reveals crucial new information on the structure of accretion flows and magnetic fields in astrophysical systems. Here, we review the basic physical processes that produce polarized X-rays in astrophysical contexts. Then, we briefly describe the physical processes used to measure X-ray polarization and the detectors that have been flown or are under construction.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how polarized X-rays are produced and detected in astrophysics, emphasizing the added value of X-ray polarimetry in studying high-energy cosmic systems.
AI.motivation: X-ray polarimetry introduces novel observables that provide unique insights into the structure of accretion flows and magnetic fields in high-energy astrophysical systems.
AI.method: The paper reviews the fundamental physical processes responsible for producing polarized X-rays and discusses the detection methods and instruments either deployed or being developed for measuring X-ray polarization.
AI.result: Identification of key physical mechanisms generating X-ray polarization and overview of existing and upcoming X-ray polarimetry detectors, highlighting their roles in astrophysical observations.
AI.conclusion: X-ray polarimetry significantly enhances our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena by adding polarization fraction and angle to the observable data, with ongoing advancements in detector technology supporting this emerging field.

title: Backreaction and the Role of Spatial Curvature in the Cosmic Neighborhood
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures
summary: We present the first direct computation of spatially averaged dynamical quantities in the local Universe, employing the Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction and a covariant scalar averaging formalism. We extract the domain-averaged density, expansion rate, spatial curvature, and kinematical backreaction over cosmologically relevant domains around our Galaxy, extending up to a comoving radius of $300~\mathrm{Mpc}/h$. The resulting domain-averaged present-day energy budget features nontrivial variations with scale that reflect a nested structure within the cosmic neighborhood, including a large-scale void shell encompassing the local cosmic web. Remarkably, we find significant contributions to this energy budget from the average spatial curvature at the $\mathcal{O}(10\%)$ level on all probed scales. By contrast, the kinematical backreaction remains much smaller throughout the surveyed volume, reaching at most a $\mathcal{O}(1\%)$ contribution on the smallest scales considered, i.e., $30~\mathrm{Mpc}/h$. Convergence to the global $Λ$CDM background is not observed within this range of scales.

AI.tldr: This study uses Cosmicflows-4++ data and scalar averaging to directly measure averaged cosmological quantities around the Milky Way up to 300 Mpc/h, finding significant spatial curvature effects and minimal kinematical backreaction, with complex local structure preventing convergence to the global ΛCDM background.
AI.motivation: To directly compute spatially averaged dynamical quantities in the local Universe using observational data and a covariant scalar averaging formalism, to better understand the energy budget on cosmological scales.
AI.method: Utilizing the Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction combined with a covariant scalar averaging formalism to extract domain-averaged quantities such as density, expansion rate, spatial curvature, and kinematical backreaction over regions around the Milky Way up to 300 Mpc/h in comoving radius.
AI.result: The analysis reveals scale-dependent variations in the domain-averaged energy budget indicative of nested cosmic structures, including a large-scale void shell. Significant average spatial curvature contributions (~10%) are found on all scales probed, while kinematical backreaction contributes less (~1%) and is only noticeable on the smallest scales. No convergence to the global ΛCDM background is observed within the studied scales.
AI.conclusion: Spatial curvature plays a non-negligible role in the local Universe's energy budget over large scales, whereas kinematical backreaction is minor. The local cosmic environment exhibits significant structural complexity that prevents convergence to the global ΛCDM model at scales up to 300 Mpc/h.

title: Multiwavelength Analysis of PSR J0437-4715 with Pulse Profile Modeling
summary: We present a multi-wavelength analysis of the nearby millisecond pulsar PSR J0437--4715, combining Hubble Space Telescope (HST) far-ultraviolet, ROSAT soft X-ray, and XMM-Newton X-ray data, to model its broadband emission and energy-resolved pulse profiles, and infer key stellar parameters via Bayesian inference. The broadband emission includes cold thermal, hot thermal, and non-thermal components: cold bulk surface emission is modeled with a non-magnetized partially-ionized hydrogen atmosphere; hot-spot emission adopts the pulse profile modeling technique with a non-magnetized fully-ionized hydrogen atmosphere model; and non-thermal emission is included as a phase-invariant power-law component. By adopting an informative prior on the hot-spot geometry informed by radio polarization position angle measurements, the joint multi-instrument analysis yields a statistically viable and radio-consistent solution with a gravitational mass of 1.38$\pm$0.03~M$_\odot$ and an equatorial circumferential radius of 13.25$_{-0.35}^{+0.34}$~km (68\% confidence intervals). The hot-spot geometry consists of two spherical caps with uniform temperature distributions: the primary hot spot is situated at a colatitude of $\approx$130$^{\circ}$, and the secondary hot spot lies at a colatitude of $\approx$9$^{\circ}$, close to the north pole. It yields tighter radius constraints than HST+ROSAT fits and shifts the radius posterior distribution to larger values relative to NICER-only fits. This work demonstrates the importance of multi-wavelength data in refining neutron star mass-radius measurements and resolving geometric degeneracies.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a Bayesian multi-wavelength analysis combining HST, ROSAT, and XMM-Newton data to refine the mass and radius measurements of PSR J0437--4715, resolving geometric uncertainties and demonstrating the advantage of integrated observations over single-instrument studies.
AI.motivation: The study aims to refine neutron star mass-radius measurements and resolve geometric degeneracies by integrating multi-wavelength data from various instruments for a comprehensive analysis of the millisecond pulsar PSR J0437--4715.
AI.method: A multi-wavelength approach combining data from HST far-ultraviolet, ROSAT soft X-ray, and XMM-Newton X-ray is employed, with the use of Bayesian inference to model broadband emission and energy-resolved pulse profiles. Emission components are modeled with hydrogen atmosphere models and a phase-invariant power-law component, and informative priors on hot-spot geometry are applied based on radio polarization measurements.
AI.result: The analysis yields a statistically viable and radio-consistent neutron star gravitational mass of 1.38±0.03 M☉ and an equatorial radius of 13.25^{+0.34}_{-0.35} km (68% confidence). The hot-spot geometry of two spherical caps at specific colatitudes is identified, with improved radius constraints compared to previous studies. The multi-wavelength analysis shifts the radius estimates to larger values relative to NICER-only results.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that multi-wavelength data integration significantly improves neutron star parameter estimation, providing tighter constraints on mass and radius and resolving ambiguities in hot-spot geometry. This highlights the critical role of combined observational data in neutron star astrophysics.

title: Self-interacting dark matter and core formation in field low-surface-brightness galaxies
comment: 16 pages
summary: Dark matter may play an important role in galaxy formation through its non-trivial properties. For example, self-interacting dark matter may contribute to the formation of the widely observed core structures in galaxies. However, galaxy formation is a complex process, and such core structures can also arise from baryonic effects within the cold dark matter framework. To clarify the role of dark matter self-interactions, it is necessary to study systems that evolve without significant baryonic disturbances. Low-surface-brightness galaxies in the field, which are gravitationally isolated and have evolved with minimal external influence, are suitable candidates for this purpose. Since these galaxies typically contain only a small amount of baryonic matter, strong baryonic effects are not expected in their evolutionary history. In this study, we assume that these galaxies decoupled from proto-clusters at high redshift. Based on this assumption, we set initial conditions and estimate the time required for core formation, which we compare with the time corresponding to the redshift of proto-clusters. We examine five low-surface-brightness galaxies in the field and three observed proto-clusters at redshifts z=2.45, 7.66 and 7.88. Our analyses, based on order-of-magnitude estimates without numerical simulations, excludes a self-interaction cross section of sigma/m = 1 cm^2/g, while sigma/m = 0.1 cm^2/g is favored. This result is consistent with constraints derived from the shapes of present-day cluster cores.

AI.tldr: This paper estimates core formation times in isolated low-surface-brightness galaxies to constrain dark matter self-interaction cross sections, favoring sigma/m = 0.1 cm^2/g over 1 cm^2/g, aligning with cluster core observations.
AI.motivation: To clarify the role of dark matter self-interactions in galaxy core formation by focusing on galaxy systems minimally affected by baryonic disturbances, specifically isolated low-surface-brightness galaxies in the field.
AI.method: The study uses order-of-magnitude estimates based on initial conditions set from the assumption that low-surface-brightness galaxies decoupled from proto-clusters at high redshift, comparing core formation times with observed proto-cluster redshifts, without employing numerical simulations.
AI.result: The analysis excludes a dark matter self-interaction cross section of sigma/m = 1 cm^2/g and supports a lower value of sigma/m = 0.1 cm^2/g, consistent with existing constraints from cluster core shapes.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a self-interaction cross section of dark matter sigma/m = 1 cm^2/g is excluded, while sigma/m = 0.1 cm^2/g is favored in explaining core structures in low-surface-brightness galaxies without significant baryonic effects.

authors: J. F. J. van den Brand
title: Searches for Binary Mergers with Sub-solar Mass Components in Data from the First Part of LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA's Fourth Observing Run
summary: We report on a gravitational wave search for compact binary coalescences involving at least one component with mass between $0.2 M_\odot$ to $1 M_\odot$, and ratio of component masses between 0.1 and 1. The analysis uses data collected by the LIGO detectors between May 24 2023 15:00 UTC and January 16 2024 16:00 UTC. No statistically significant sub-solar mass candidates were identified by the participating search algorithms. We report the detection sensitivity of the current searches to the target sub-solar mass black hole population, while also reporting the sensitivity of the search to low-mass neutron star binaries for the first time. With the absence of detections, we place upper limits on the merger rate of sub-solar mass black holes, ranging from $110$ $\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$ to $10000$ $\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$ at 90% confidence. We use the merger rate limits to constrain two illustrative dark matter scenarios that can form sub-solar mass compact objects: primordial black holes, and dark black holes forming in a dissipative dark matter model. For late-forming primordial black hole binaries, our search excludes the fraction of dark matter in primordial black holes to be 1 for masses above $0.9 M_\odot$. In the early-formation scenario, we limit this fraction to be $\leq$ 7% at $1 M_\odot$, and $\leq$ 40% at $0.35 M_\odot$. For the dissipative model, the excluded region in the parameter space of dark matter fraction in dark black holes and their minimum possible mass extends down to (1.2 to 1.3) $\times10^{-5}$ when the minimum mass is $1 M_\odot$. For binary neutron stars that include sub-solar mass components, we estimate the sensitive space-time hypervolume to be $10^{-3}$ $\mathrm{Gpc^3yr}$, and report the upper limit on their merger rate for a simple, fixed population as ~86 $\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$.

AI.tldr: LIGO data analysis found no gravitational wave signals from sub-solar mass compact binaries, setting upper limits on merger rates and constraining dark matter models involving primordial and dissipative black holes.
AI.motivation: To search for gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences involving at least one sub-solar mass component, motivated by the possibility of detecting exotic objects like primordial or dark matter black holes.
AI.method: Analyzed data from LIGO detectors collected between May 24, 2023 and January 16, 2024, using search algorithms targeting binaries with component masses between 0.2 and 1 solar masses and mass ratios between 0.1 and 1.
AI.result: No significant sub-solar mass candidates were found. Upper limits on merger rates of sub-solar mass black holes were set, constraining their population and dark matter scenarios like primordial black holes and dissipative dark matter models. Sensitivity to low-mass neutron star binaries was reported along with upper limits on their merger rate.
AI.conclusion: The null detection allows meaningful constraints on the fraction of dark matter composed of sub-solar mass black holes under different formation scenarios, and on merger rates of sub-solar mass neutron star binaries, advancing our understanding of compact objects below one solar mass.

title: Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation for astrophysical model comparison using gravitational-wave background data
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures
summary: Previous work showed that ultralight-dark-matter solitons can provide dynamical friction for supermassive black-hole binaries, suppressing low-frequency power in the pulsar-timing-array gravitational-wave background and constraining the particle mass and effective ultralight-dark-matter fraction. Here we extend that analysis by comparing the predictive performance of four models: simplified and realistic ultralight-dark-matter implementations, a phenomenological environmental-hardening model, and a gravitational-wave-only model. We use Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on the five lowest pulsar-timing-array frequency bins. The phenomenological model gives the largest expected log predictive density, but its advantage over the other models is not large compared with the estimated standard errors. The current data therefore do not decisively prefer one model overall. The clearest pairwise result is within the ultralight-dark-matter framework: the simplified model outperforms the realistic implementation in all five frequency bins. Current pulsar-timing-array data are therefore compatible with ultralight-dark-matter-induced low-frequency suppression, but do not yet distinguish ultralight-dark-matter significantly from more generic environmental descriptions of supermassive-black-hole-binary evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper compares models explaining low-frequency gravitational-wave suppression in pulsar-timing data, finding no decisive preference among them, though simplified ULDM models perform better than realistic ones. Present data are compatible with ULDM effects but cannot definitively confirm or exclude them relative to other environmental scenarios.
AI.motivation: To extend previous work on ultralight-dark-matter (ULDM) effects on supermassive black-hole binaries and their imprint on the pulsar-timing-array gravitational-wave background, improving model comparisons to constrain ULDM properties.
AI.method: Comparison of four models—simplified and realistic ULDM implementations, a phenomenological environmental-hardening model, and a gravitational-wave-only model—using Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on the five lowest frequency bins from pulsar-timing-array data.
AI.result: The phenomenological model has the highest expected log predictive density but is not significantly better than others given uncertainties. The simplified ULDM model outperforms the realistic ULDM model consistently across frequency bins. Current data do not decisively favor any model over others, indicating compatibility with ULDM-induced effects but no significant distinction from generic environmental models.
AI.conclusion: Pulsar-timing-array data are consistent with ULDM-induced low-frequency gravitational-wave suppression but lack the statistical power to conclusively distinguish ULDM effects from alternative environmental mechanisms affecting supermassive-black-hole-binary evolution.

title: A Multiwavelength Assessment Disfavoring the X-ray Binary Origin of He III Regions in Metal-Poor Star-Forming Dwarf Galaxies
summary: Recent observations of metal-poor, star-forming dwarf galaxies reveal He III regions, traced by nebular He II 4686 emission that require a strong source of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) radiation. The origin of this hard ionizing radiation remains poorly understood, as standard stellar populations fail to account for it, posing key implications for the understanding of early galaxy formation. We present a systematic Chandra X-ray study of 21 nearby star-forming galaxies with He II emission but lacking Wolf-Rayet spectral signatures. Using 7 new and 36 archival Chandra X-ray observations combined with optical stellar population synthesis modelling, we constrain the ionizing continuum required to sustain the observed He II line, the ionizing continuum available from X-ray objects, and the properties of the host H II regions. We find that the inferred EUV output from accreting X-ray sources in our sample is systematically lower than what is required to produce the observed He II emission. Our sample is consistent with established empirical scaling relations for X-ray luminosity, indicating that this discrepancy cannot be attributed to an anomalously low number or luminosity of X-ray sources. These results indicate that accreting X-ray sources alone cannot account for the observed He II-ionizing photon budget, pointing to additional or alternative sources of hard EUV radiation in metal-poor star-forming environments. Potential alternative or additional contributors are discussed.

AI.tldr: X-ray sources in metal-poor star-forming galaxies do not emit enough extreme-ultraviolet radiation to account for observed He II emission, suggesting other sources contribute to the hard ionizing radiation required for He III regions.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of hard extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) radiation required to produce He III regions in metal-poor, star-forming dwarf galaxies, which is not explained by standard stellar populations.
AI.method: Systematic Chandra X-ray study of 21 nearby star-forming galaxies with He II emission but lacking Wolf-Rayet signatures, combining 7 new and 36 archival Chandra X-ray observations with optical stellar population synthesis modeling to constrain ionizing continuum and X-ray source properties.
AI.result: Accreting X-ray sources in the sample produce systematically lower EUV output than required to sustain observed He II emission; the sample matches empirical X-ray luminosity scaling relations, indicating that the discrepancy is not due to lack of X-ray sources or luminosity.
AI.conclusion: Accreting X-ray sources alone cannot explain the observed He II-ionizing photon budget in metal-poor star-forming galaxies, implying additional or alternative sources of hard EUV radiation are necessary.

title: From Scalar $H_0$ to $E(z)$: A Reformulation of the Hubble Tension
comment: 17pages, 1figure
summary: The Hubble tension is usually expressed as a discrepancy between the low H_0 inferred from Planck CMB data within base \LambdaCDM and the higher value obtained from late-time distance-ladder measurements. This scalar comparison compresses distinct inference problems into one derived parameter: Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+SH0ES constrain physical densities and acoustic scales, ruler-normalized distances, and calibrated luminosity-distance relations, respectively. We reformulate the comparison in terms of the dimensionless expansion history E(z)=H(z)/H_0. This does not remove the absolute-scale discrepancy, but separates the normalization encoded in $H_0$ from the redshift-dependent shape of the expansion history. Within a common flat-\LambdaCDM framework, each probe posterior is mapped onto posterior-implied E(z) histories. Since the reconstructed values E(z_k) are strongly correlated across redshift, we quantify the global mismatch with a covariance-subspace history displacement S_{hist}, alongside pointwise redshift differences. The histories are not identical, but the discrepancies are moderate: the pointwise significance is typically 1-2σ, while S_{hist} simeq 1.65 for DESI DR2 and S_{hist} \simeq 2.55 for Pantheon+SH0ES relative to Planck. With two retained covariance eigenmodes, these correspond to two-sided one-dimensional Gaussian equivalents of approximately 1.1σand 2.1σ, both below the conventional \simeq 4.9σPlanck-SH0ES scalar-H_0 discrepancy.

AI.tldr: This study reformulates the Hubble tension using the dimensionless expansion history to separate shape and normalization effects, showing that discrepancies between Planck, DESI DR2, and Pantheon+SH0ES data are moderate and lower in significance than the usual H_0 scalar comparison suggests.
AI.motivation: To address the Hubble tension by decomposing the discrepancy between early- and late-time measurements of the Hubble constant into its expansion history shape and normalization components.
AI.method: Reformulate the Hubble tension comparison using the dimensionless expansion history E(z)=H(z)/H_0, mapping posterior distributions from Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+SH0ES measurements onto E(z) histories, and quantify discrepancies using a covariance-subspace displacement metric S_hist alongside pointwise redshift differences.
AI.result: Found moderate discrepancies in the reconstructed expansion histories with pointwise significance typically 1-2σ, and global mismatch metrics S_hist approximately 1.65 (DESI DR2) and 2.55 (Pantheon+SH0ES) relative to Planck, corresponding to lower tensions (~1.1σ and ~2.1σ) than the previously reported ~4.9σ H_0 scalar discrepancy.
AI.conclusion: Separating the normalization parameter H_0 from the redshift-dependent expansion history shape reduces the Hubble tension significance, revealing only moderate mismatches across probes within a flat-9CDM framework, thus indicating that the tension may be less severe than traditionally expressed by direct H_0 comparisons.

title: How do the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's Heavy Black Holes Form? No evidence for core-collapse Intermediate-mass black holes in GWTC-4
comment: 15pages, 8figures(4 in main text and 4 in appendix)
summary: We investigate the population properties of binary black holes (BBHs) from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, focusing especially on those in the high-mass range, using the newly released GWTC-4 catalog. For the first time, we search for a subpopulation of low-spin intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) that would indicate formation via stellar core collapse. With the currently available catalog, we find no evidence for such a subpopulation, and set a 90\% upper limit on the merger rate of collapse-formed IMBHs at $0.077~\mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The mass distribution of low-spin (stellar-origin) black holes truncates at $65^{+23}_{-22}\,M_\odot$, consistent with the lower edge of the pair-instability mass gap (PIMG), although we cannot directly determine its upper boundary from current data. Informed by stellar evolution theory, we estimate the upper edge of the PIMG to be $150\pm24\,M_\odot$. We find that the observed IMBHs belong to a high-spin subpopulation, consistent with formation through successive hierarchical mergers.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA GWTC-4 data and finds no low-spin IMBHs from stellar core collapse. The low-spin BH mass distribution aligns with the predicted pair-instability mass gap, while observed IMBHs exhibit high spins consistent with formation via hierarchical mergers.
AI.motivation: To explore the population properties of binary black holes detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA, particularly focusing on the high-mass range and searching for a subpopulation of low-spin intermediate-mass black holes indicative of stellar core collapse formation.
AI.method: Analysis of the GWTC-4 gravitational wave catalog data to identify and characterize subpopulations of black holes based on their mass and spin properties, incorporating constraints from stellar evolution theory.
AI.result: No evidence was found for a low-spin intermediate-mass black hole subpopulation formed via stellar core collapse. A 90% upper limit on the merger rate for such black holes was set at 0.077 Gpc^{-3} yr^{-1}. The low-spin stellar-origin black hole mass distribution truncates near 65^{+23}_{-22} solar masses, consistent with the lower edge of the pair-instability mass gap. The upper edge of the mass gap was estimated at 150±24 solar masses. Observed intermediate-mass black holes were identified as part of a high-spin subpopulation consistent with hierarchical merger formation.
AI.conclusion: The current gravitational wave data show no support for a low-spin intermediate-mass black hole population formed by stellar core collapse, instead indicating that observed IMBHs likely arise from hierarchical mergers, with the stellar-origin black hole mass distribution consistent with theoretical pair-instability mass gap boundaries.

title: Axion-Like Particle Dark Matter Intensity Mapping: A New Probe via Cross-Correlation with Galaxy Surveys
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, two tables. Accepted for publication in PLB
summary: The particle nature of dark matter (DM) remains one of the most significant enigmas in modern cosmology. Axion-like particles (ALPs), as well-motivated candidates for cold dark matter, can undergo radiative decay into photon pairs, a process that is significantly enhanced in the presence of ambient radiation fields. In this work, we propose a novel probe of $μ{\rm eV}$-scale ALP DM by cross-correlating radio intensity mapping (IM) with the large-scale galaxy distribution from the 2MASS Redshift Survey (2MRS) in the local universe ($z\leq 0.1$). We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that incorporates stimulated decay effects driven by both the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and a bottom-up modeled extragalactic radio background (ERB). By forecasting the sensitivity of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) Phase 2, we demonstrate that this cross-correlation technique provides a promising and complementary approach to searching for ALP DM signals. This study establishes a new proof-of-concept for utilizing next-generation radio telescopes to probe ALP dark matter on cosmic scales.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and theoretically develops a new method to detect micro-eV axion-like particle dark matter by cross-correlating radio intensity maps with galaxy distributions, demonstrating promising sensitivity with future SKA observations.
AI.motivation: To address the significant enigma of the particle nature of dark matter and specifically explore axion-like particles (ALPs) as promising cold dark matter candidates.
AI.method: Proposing a novel probe by cross-correlating radio intensity mapping with large-scale galaxy distribution data (2MASS Redshift Survey), incorporating stimulated decay effects driven by the CMB and modeled extragalactic radio background; sensitivity forecast for the SKA Phase 2 was performed.
AI.result: The cross-correlation technique using next-generation radio telescopes like SKA Phase 2 shows promising sensitivity and provides a complementary approach to searching for ALP dark matter signals at micro-eV scale.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a new proof-of-concept for using radio telescopes to detect ALP dark matter via stimulated radiative decay, opening a novel observational window for cosmic-scale ALP DM detection.

title: An Insight-HXMT View of the Evolution of the Type-C Quasiperiodic Oscillation during the Flaring State of Swift J1727.8-1613
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the evolution of type-C quasiperiodic oscillations (QPOs) observed during the flaring state of the recently discovered black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8-1613, utilizing data from the Insight Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope. By examining the relation between the QPO fractional rms amplitude and QPO frequency across various energy bands, we discover that the behavior significantly differs between these energy bands. Below 10 keV, the QPO fractional rms generally decreases with increasing QPO frequency, whereas above 10 keV, the QPO fractional rms remains relatively stable with frequency. Additionally, we report, for the first time, the detection of a common break at around 4 Hz in the relation between QPO fractional rms and frequency in both the 2-4 and 50-100 keV energy bands. We also find that the evolution of all the spectral parameters alters its behavior at around 4 Hz, with the changes in all parameters becoming flatter. This suggests a significant change in the geometry of the accretion flow. We attribute the observed break to the overall changes in the spectrum.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes type-C QPOs in Swift J1727.8-1613, revealing energy-dependent rms-frequency behaviors and a novel 4 Hz break suggesting a key change in the accretion flow geometry during flaring.
AI.motivation: To understand the evolution and energy-dependent behavior of type-C quasiperiodic oscillations (QPOs) in the black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8-1613 during its flaring state.
AI.method: Analysis of QPO fractional rms amplitude and frequency relation across multiple energy bands using data from the Insight Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope.
AI.result: Identification of differing QPO fractional rms behavior below and above 10 keV; discovery of a common break at ~4 Hz in the rms-frequency relation in both low (2-4 keV) and high (50-100 keV) energy bands; spectral parameters show a flattening evolution around the break frequency.
AI.conclusion: The observed 4 Hz break and associated changes in spectral parameter behavior indicate a significant geometric alteration in the accretion flow of Swift J1727.8-1613, linked to the overall spectral evolution.

title: Revisiting the Constancy of the Speed of Light: Galaxy Cluster Mass Bias Implications
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Paper published in Astroparticle Physics (180, 2026, 103249)
summary: In recent years, improvements in galaxy cluster observations have enabled a variety of tests of fundamental physics using these systems. In this work, we test the constancy of the speed of light, $c$, by combining X-ray gas mass fraction measurements from galaxy clusters with SNe Ia luminosity distance measurements from Pantheon+. We adopt the SH0ES prior on $H_0$ and the $Ω_b/Ω_m$ ratio from galaxy clustering observations, thereby minimizing the dependence of our analysis on any specific cosmological model. We explore different assumptions for the cluster mass calibration (mass bias), including \textsc{CLASH}, \textsc{CCCP}, and Planck-based estimates. We find no deviation from a constant $c$ when adopting \textsc{CLASH} or \textsc{CCCP} priors, while Planck-based calibration yields a mild tension, with the hypothesis of constant $c$ being only marginally consistent at the $2σ$ level, indicating a non-negligible sensitivity of the results to the adopted calibration scheme.

AI.tldr: This study tests the constancy of the speed of light using galaxy cluster and supernova data, finding consistency except when using Planck-based cluster mass calibration which shows mild tension.
AI.motivation: To test the constancy of the speed of light using galaxy cluster and supernova data with minimal cosmological model dependence.
AI.method: Combining X-ray gas mass fraction measurements from galaxy clusters with Type Ia supernova luminosity distances, adopting SH0ES prior on H0 and baryon-to-matter ratio from galaxy clustering, while exploring different cluster mass calibration schemes.
AI.result: No deviation from constant speed of light found with CLASH or CCCP mass calibrations; Planck-based calibration shows mild tension with constancy hypothesis at 2-sigma level.
AI.conclusion: The constancy of the speed of light is supported by most calibration choices, but results are sensitive to the cluster mass calibration method, highlighting the importance of systematic uncertainties in such tests.

title: Tearing of charged current layers
summary: Astrophysical current layers, e.g., in pulsar winds, can be electrically charged, while the plasma is charge-symmetric, $e^\pm$. Using PIC simulations, we investigate dynamics and plasmoid formation (tearing instability) in charged Harris-type and rotational current layers. Electrically charged current layers, initially in global force-balance, are electrostatically unstable: the resulting dynamics is an intricate interplay between electrostatic Bernstein waves (BWs) and the current tearing mode. Besides overall density and magnetic field, plasma temperature is an important factor. In the charged Harris sheet set-up, the quickly generated BW are trapped within the layers (internally reflected at the upper hybrid resonance). BWs quickly redistribute the charge modifying the initial stage of tearing, but without strongly affecting overall plasmoid growth; resulting plasmoids are mildly charged. In rotational current layers: (i) even initially overall uncharged configurations develop large fluctuations of charge density; (ii) overall dynamics depends on the initial overall temperature; (iii) for certain combination of parameters tearing rate is greatly increased in the charged case.

AI.tldr: This study uses PIC simulations to show that charge and plasma temperature critically impact instabilities and plasmoid formation in astrophysical current layers, revealing electrostatic instabilities and charge fluctuations that influence tearing dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand the effects of electric charge on the dynamics and plasmoid formation in astrophysical current layers that are charge-symmetric in plasma composition.
AI.method: Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations were used to study the dynamics and plasmoid formation in charged Harris-type and rotational current layers, focusing on the interplay between electrostatic Bernstein waves and the tearing mode.
AI.result: Electrically charged current layers exhibit electrostatic instability, with Bernstein waves redistributing charge and affecting the initial tearing phase. Plasmoid growth remains largely unaffected and results in mildly charged plasmoids in the Harris sheet. In rotational layers, even initially uncharged states develop charge density fluctuations, with dynamics dependent on plasma temperature, and certain parameters cause significantly increased tearing rates in charged cases.
AI.conclusion: Charged current layers in astrophysical plasmas are electrostatically unstable due to Bernstein waves influencing the early tearing instability stage, with plasma temperature playing a critical role; this leads to charged plasmoids and can enhance tearing rates under specific conditions.

title: Galaxy clusters in the LoTSS-DR3: Catalogues and detection pipeline for diffuse radio emission
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables, accepted by A&A
summary: The third data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey provides an unprecedented view of the northern sky at 144 MHz. While compact sources can be efficiently identified with automated software packages, the detection of diffuse radio emission associated with galaxy clusters still requires dedicated processing and visual inspection. Given the scale of current and forthcoming radio surveys, automated approaches based on artificial intelligence are becoming essential to the identification of the most interesting targets. We aim to develop an automated pipeline to construct a catalogue of galaxy clusters hosting diffuse radio emission from LoTSS-DR3 20arcsec images. The pipeline is designed to provide both the probability that a cluster hosts diffuse radio emission and an interpretable image of its shape and morphology. We employed Radio U-Net, a convolutional neural network optimised for image segmentation (i.e. pixel-level identification) of diffuse radio emission. To associate detected emission with individual clusters, we combined the network output with positional, mass, and redshift information from four X-ray- and Sunyaev-Zeldovich-selected cluster catalogues, resulting in a merged sample of 3822 clusters covered by the LoTSS-DR3. We produced a pixel-level segmentation map of the full LoTSS-DR3 and a quantitative indicator for the presence of diffuse emission in each cluster. This enables the selection of sub-samples with specific properties for targeted follow-up or statistical studies. As a demonstration of the first application, we identified a sub-sample of 357 clusters selected at the highest network accuracy (76%), and we showed some examples of newly detected systems. For the second, using a larger statistical sample, we verified that the detection fraction of diffuse radio sources in the four catalogues increases with the mass and redshift of the clusters. [Abridged]

AI.tldr: An AI-driven pipeline using Radio U-Net segments diffuse radio emissions in LOFAR survey images, linking them to galaxy clusters with cluster data to create a catalogue of over 3800 clusters, enabling accurate detection and analysis of diffuse emissions, validated by new detections and trends with cluster mass and redshift.
AI.motivation: To automate the detection of diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters from large-scale radio surveys, overcoming the limitations of manual visual inspection for efficient identification of interesting targets.
AI.method: Developed an automated pipeline utilizing Radio U-Net, a convolutional neural network optimized for pixel-level image segmentation of diffuse radio emission in LoTSS-DR3 20arcsec images. The network output was combined with positional, mass, and redshift data from four cluster catalogues to associate emissions with specific clusters, producing pixel-level segmentation maps and quantitative presence indicators.
AI.result: Generated a catalogue of 3822 galaxy clusters with probabilistic and morphological information of diffuse radio emission. Identified a high-confidence sub-sample of 357 clusters with 76% accuracy, discovered new systems, and established that detection fraction increases with cluster mass and redshift, validating the approach statistically.
AI.conclusion: The automated pipeline effectively identifies diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters with interpretable morphological output, enabling efficient cataloguing and study of cluster radio properties in large-scale surveys, and supports targeted follow-up and statistical analyses.

title: A comparative study of occurrence rates and nature of Ultraluminous X-ray sources in spiral and elliptical galaxies
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures
summary: Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are mostly extragalactic non-nuclear point sources having X-ray luminosity exceeding the Eddington luminosity of 10 $M_\odot$ black hole i.e., $L_X \geq $ 10$^{39}$ erg ~s$^{-1}$. They are observed in all types of galaxies; spirals, ellipticals and dwarf irregulars. But the rate of occurrence of ULXs per galaxy varies, some might host a single ULX, whereas some host a large number. In this work we attempt to identify possible differences in ULX properties between two extreme categories in spirals and ellipticals, i.e. ULXs occurring at a rate of one per galaxy ($N=1$) and those occurring at larger rate. We adopt an effective scheme to generate flux limited, credible samples corresponding to the two groups in spirals and ellipticals. From this study, we infer the presence of a separate population of ULXs in the $N=1$ spiral group which contains a reasonable fraction of both soft and hard sources, while the remaining categories contain mostly harder sources. We also find six ULXs in $N=1$ ellipticals with globular cluster association. In addition, we identify few luminous candidates likely hosting massive accretors. This study provides crucial hints of a potential link between ULX types and their occurrence rates and host morphology, a finding that warrants validation via targeted observations and detailed spectral analysis of these sources.

AI.tldr: The study reveals distinct populations of ULXs in spiral and elliptical galaxies based on ULX occurrence rates, highlighting a link between ULX types, their frequency, and host galaxy morphology, which needs further observational confirmation.
AI.motivation: To identify differences in properties of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) between galaxies hosting a single ULX and those hosting multiple ULXs, particularly in spiral and elliptical galaxies.
AI.method: Generated flux-limited, credible samples of ULXs divided into two groups based on occurrence rate (one ULX per galaxy and multiple ULXs per galaxy) within spiral and elliptical galaxies for comparative analysis.
AI.result: Detected a distinct population of ULXs in spiral galaxies hosting only one ULX per galaxy, composed of both soft and hard sources, while other categories mainly contain hard sources. Found six ULXs in elliptical galaxies with globular cluster associations and identified several luminous candidates likely containing massive accretors.
AI.conclusion: There exists a potential link between ULX types, their occurrence rates, and host galaxy morphology, suggesting different ULX populations depending on galaxy type and ULX frequency. This relationship requires further validation through targeted observations and detailed spectral analysis.

authors: the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration
title: Constraining Galaxy Cluster Triaxiality via Weak Lensing -- I. Preparation for the Rubin Data Beyond Leading Order
comment: 31 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The 3D mass distributions of galaxy clusters are generally triaxial, a geometry that is difficult to constrain from projected observations. In this work, we measure the projected halo shapes of clusters from their weak lensing signatures using the triaxiality functionality in the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling software, a tool developed by the Dark Energy Science Collaboration to analyze data from NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We measure ensemble halo ellipticity on the plane of the sky via axis-aligned stacking and multipole expansion of the weak lensing data. We study a precursor dataset -- the redMaPPer cluster catalog, the metacalibration shape catalog, and the Directional Neighborhood Fitting photometric redshift catalog from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 public data release. We select clusters that have a high centering probability (>90%) of the identified central galaxy, and use the satellite galaxy distribution to determine the major-axis orientation for stacking. We extend the analysis to the second order of ellipticity in the monopole and quadrupole measurement. The projected ellipticity of the cluster sample is found to be $0.310^{+0.017}_{-0.016}$ (axis ratio $0.527^{+0.018}_{-0.019}$). The projected cluster ellipticity shows no statistically significant dependence on mass and redshift. We further verify the accuracy of the cluster shape measurement using mock catalogs. This analysis is applicable to datasets from upcoming wide-area cosmic surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope, where larger sample sizes will lead to tighter constraints on the cluster ellipticities.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the projected shapes of galaxy clusters using weak lensing data and a triaxiality modeling tool on DES Y3 data, finding a mean ellipticity of ~0.31 with no redshift or mass dependence, validated by simulations, and anticipating tighter constraints from upcoming surveys.
AI.motivation: To better constrain the generally triaxial 3D mass distributions of galaxy clusters using their projected observational data, which is challenging due to projection effects.
AI.method: Measured projected halo shapes using weak lensing signatures with the triaxiality functionality in the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling software; utilized axis-aligned stacking and multipole expansion of weak lensing data; applied to data from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3, selecting well-centered clusters and using satellite galaxy distribution to fix major-axis orientation; extended analysis to second-order ellipticity in monopole and quadrupole measurements.
AI.result: Found the projected ellipticity of the cluster sample to be 0.310 (+0.017/-0.016) corresponding to an axis ratio of 0.527 (+0.018/-0.019); no statistically significant dependence of ellipticity on cluster mass or redshift; validated shape measurements with mock catalogs.
AI.conclusion: The method effectively constrains projected cluster ellipticities from weak lensing data and is suitable for application to future large-scale surveys like LSST, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope, where increased sample sizes will improve ellipticity constraints.

title: Vacuum polarization and cyclotron resonance effects on radiative transfer and plasma deceleration in subcritical X-ray pulsars
comment: 20 pages, 14 figures, 1 table (to be submitted to MNRAS; comments are welcome)
summary: We investigate the spectrum and polarization of radiation emerging from a subcritical X-ray pulsar using self-consistent radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of an accretion channel in a strong magnetic field. The polarized radiative transfer in the channel above the hot spot is simulated for the two normal modes, taking into account resonant Compton scattering in a strongly magnetized plasma and the effects of vacuum polarization. We show that the deceleration of the accreting matter in the subcritical regime is mainly governed by resonant scattering. Our simulations provide the velocity profiles of the plasma flow and demonstrate that vacuum polarization dominates over plasma birefringence, enhancing both the cyclotron spectral feature and the radiative deceleration of the plasma. The linear polarization degree changes sign at photon energies above the cyclotron resonance when vacuum polarization is included. We also find that the centroid energy of the cyclotron scattering feature increases with accretion luminosity, indicating a positive correlation consistent with previous observational results and theoretical interpretation.

AI.tldr: This study models radiation and polarization in subcritical X-ray pulsars, revealing that vacuum polarization enhances cyclotron features and plasma deceleration, and that cyclotron line energy increases with luminosity, aligning with observations.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectrum and polarization characteristics of radiation from subcritical X-ray pulsars in strong magnetic fields, accounting for complex plasma and vacuum effects.
AI.method: Self-consistent radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the accretion channel, coupled with polarized radiative transfer modeling including resonant Compton scattering and vacuum polarization effects for the two normal modes.
AI.result: The deceleration of accreting matter is primarily driven by resonant scattering; vacuum polarization effects dominate plasma birefringence, enhancing cyclotron spectral features and plasma deceleration; the linear polarization degree sign changes above cyclotron resonance; and the cyclotron feature's centroid energy positively correlates with accretion luminosity.
AI.conclusion: Vacuum polarization significantly influences the radiation spectrum and polarization in subcritical X-ray pulsars, affecting plasma deceleration and spectral features, consistent with observational data on cyclotron resonance energy behavior with luminosity.

title: Early interaction signatures and an extended plateau phase in Type II SN 2020aze
comment: 16 pages, 16 figures and 10 tables
summary: We present a photometric and spectroscopic analysis of the fast-declining Type II SN 2020aze, observed in optical bands from 2.2 to 137.4 days after explosion. The V-band light curve reaches a peak absolute magnitude of about minus 16.97$\pm$0.20 mag by 15 days, followed by a recombination phase with a decline rate of 2.04$\pm$0.13 mag per 100 days, lasting about 120 days. Early spectra (younger than 6 days) show a transient weak narrow emission line at 4687 Angstroms and a feature spanning 4400-4800 Angstroms, attributed to narrow and broad blue-shifted He II 4686, indicating interaction between the ejecta and dense circumstellar material. Comparison with spectral models suggests a red supergiant progenitor with a weak wind and a mass-loss rate of about 1e-3 solar masses per year. Semi-analytical light-curve modeling gives an initial radius of about 1100 solar radii, an ejecta mass of about 12 solar masses, an explosion energy of about 1.5e51 erg, and a progenitor mass of about 14 solar masses. These early interaction signatures, the steep decline, and the extended photospheric phase highlight the role of pre-supernova mass loss and circumstellar interaction in shaping the diversity of Type II supernovae.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the fast-declining Type II SN 2020aze's light curve and spectra, revealing early ejecta interaction with circumstellar material from a red supergiant progenitor. Modeling estimates the progenitor's properties and highlights how mass loss and circumstellar interaction drive diversity in Type II supernovae.
AI.motivation: To investigate the characteristics and diversity of fast-declining Type II supernovae, specifically exploring the role of pre-supernova mass loss and circumstellar interaction.
AI.method: Photometric monitoring in optical bands from 2.2 to 137.4 days post-explosion combined with spectroscopic observations to identify emission features and spectral evolution; comparison with spectral models to infer progenitor properties; semi-analytical light-curve modeling to estimate physical parameters such as progenitor radius, ejecta mass, explosion energy, and progenitor mass.
AI.result: Identification of a fast-declining V-band light curve with a specific peak magnitude and decline rate; detection of early spectral features indicative of interaction between ejecta and dense circumstellar material; spectral modeling suggesting a red supergiant progenitor with weak wind and a mass-loss rate of ~1e-3 solar masses per year; light-curve modeling results estimating progenitor radius (~1100 solar radii), ejecta mass (~12 solar masses), explosion energy (~1.5e51 erg), and progenitor mass (~14 solar masses); recognition that early circumstellar interaction and pre-supernova mass loss influence Type II SN diversity.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that pre-supernova mass loss and circumstellar material interaction significantly affect the photometric and spectroscopic evolution of fast-declining Type II supernovae, emphasizing their importance in shaping the observed diversity of these events.

title: Gravitational Lensing of Gravitational Waves from Astrophysical Sources: Theory, Detection, and Applications
comment: 47 pages (single-column preprint), 8 figures. Invited Review for Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics (RAA)
summary: Gravitational waves (GWs) from distant sources such as inspiralling and merging stellar-mass compact binaries, intermediate-mass and supermassive-binary-black-hole can be gravitationally lensed by intervening objects, ranging from stars and primordial black holes to galaxies and clusters. Depending on the GW wavelength relative to the lens scale, lensing occurs in two regimes: geometric optics, producing multiple images with time delays and magnifications, and wave optics, resulting in frequency-dependent waveform modulations. Lensed signals are identified via parameter overlap between event pairs or characteristic frequency-dependent modulations that distinguish them from unlensed signals. Detection rates depend on the redshift and mass distributions of sources and lenses, with promising prospects for future observatories. Once confirmed, lensed GWs will be powerful probes of fundamental physics and cosmology: they can constrain dark matter, lensing structures, the Hubble constant, and other cosmological parameters. In this review, we provide a concise overview of GW lensing, covering the theoretical framework, predicted detection rates, search strategies, and applications. We conclude with prospects and future directions for observing and exploiting lensed astrophysical GW events.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes gravitational wave lensing theory, detection methods, expected rates, and scientific applications, highlighting its potential for upcoming observatories to advance cosmology and fundamental physics.
AI.motivation: To explore the phenomenon of gravitational wave lensing caused by various intervening objects and its implications for astrophysics and cosmology.
AI.method: Review of theoretical frameworks of gravitational wave lensing, analysis of detection strategies, rate predictions, and applications in fundamental physics and cosmology.
AI.result: Identification of two lensing regimes (geometric and wave optics), methods for detecting lensed gravitational wave signals, predicted detection rates for future observatories, and potential constraints on dark matter, lensing structures, and cosmological parameters.
AI.conclusion: Gravitational wave lensing offers a promising avenue for probing fundamental physics and cosmology. Future gravitational wave observatories are expected to detect these events, enabling constraints on dark matter, lensing structures, and cosmological parameters such as the Hubble constant.

title: Fifteen new millisecond pulsars in 47 Tucanae
summary: 47 Tucanae is one of the largest, brightest, and closest globular clusters to Earth. It hosts an exotic stellar population with stellar dynamics that indicate a complex evolution history. The cluster contains a large number of X-ray binaries and millisecond pulsars. However, given its large distance relative to the known pulsar population, previous surveys have found only the very brightest sources. Therefore, surveys with increased sensitivity should find many additional pulsars. Increasing the number of pulsars is crucial to investigate the dynamics of this globular cluster and could also lead to the discovery of unusual types of system. With a significantly increased sensitivity compared to earlier telescopes, MeerKAT is the natural choice to perform new surveys. We carried out two campaigns with different observational cadences to account for the high scintillation along the line of sight to this cluster. Here we report the discovery of fifteen new pulsars in 47 Tucanae with MeerKAT. These discoveries bring the total number of known pulsars in this globular cluster to 42, and the MeerKAT discoveries in this cluster to 17. We discuss some of their characteristics, which include preliminary localisations and estimates of orbits for most systems. Highlights include the discovery of 47 Tuc af, a 'black widow' pulsar with a short orbital period that was identified optically in 2002 as a candidate binary pulsar, and 47 Tuc ai, an eccentric binary pulsar with a massive companion, a unique system in 47 Tuc to date. Apart from the new systems, we also re-detect and localise 47 Tuc P and V, two elusive, seldom-detected systems that had no precise localisation from a phase-connected timing solution. The localisation of 47 Tuc V places it in a position consistent with a continuum source detected earlier in MeerKAT imaging data.

AI.tldr: Using MeerKAT's improved sensitivity and carefully planned observations, fifteen new pulsars were discovered in 47 Tucanae, significantly increasing the known population and providing valuable data on unique pulsar systems within this globular cluster.
AI.motivation: Previous surveys of 47 Tucanae had limited sensitivity and only detected the brightest pulsars; increasing the number of detected pulsars is crucial to understanding the cluster's dynamics and discovering unusual systems.
AI.method: Conducted two observational campaigns with the MeerKAT telescope using different cadences to mitigate scintillation effects and increase sensitivity over previous surveys.
AI.result: Discovered fifteen new pulsars in 47 Tucanae, bringing the total known pulsars to 42 in the cluster, including unique systems such as a 'black widow' pulsar and an eccentric binary pulsar with a massive companion; also re-detected and precisely localized two elusive pulsars.
AI.conclusion: MeerKAT's enhanced sensitivity and observational strategy effectively expanded the known pulsar population in 47 Tucanae, enabling better insights into the cluster's stellar dynamics and revealing rare binary pulsar systems.
